issues.legal_issue: A constitutional amendment made through the prescribed amendment process is law subject to the Constitution’s protection of fundamental rights.
material_facts: The petitions challenged constitutional amendments that changed provisions protecting property and placed land-reform statutes beyond challenge under Part III.
The Court examined the relationship between the amendment procedure and the prohibition on laws taking away or abridging fundamental rights.
issues.conclusion: A constitutional amendment is law for the purposes of the fundamental-rights prohibition, and an amendment that takes away or abridges fundamental rights is subject to that prohibition.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the amendment procedure in Article 368 does not itself confer the power to amend; the power derives from the legislative powers in Articles 245, 246 and 248, while Article 368 prescribes the procedure. Because an amendment is made through a legislative process, it is law within Article 13(2). The Court rejected the contrary reasoning in Sri Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India and Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan on this point.

predicates.constitutional_amendment_challenged: A party challenged the validity of a constitutional amendment in court.
predicates.amendment_made_through_amendment_process: The amendment was enacted through the constitutionally prescribed process for changing the Constitution.

issues.definition: When a constitutional amendment is challenged and was made through the prescribed amendment process, it is treated as subject to the fundamental-rights bar.

issues.legal_issue: Parliament cannot amend the Constitution to take away or abridge fundamental rights.
material_facts: The amendments under challenge altered protections for property and protected land-reform legislation from challenges based on fundamental rights.
The Court reconsidered earlier decisions that had recognized Parliament’s power to amend Part III.
issues.conclusion: Parliament has no power to amend Part III so as to take away or abridge fundamental rights.
issues.legal_principle: Article 13(2) prohibits the State from making law that takes away or abridges rights in Part III. The Court held that this prohibition applies to constitutional amendments and overruled the contrary view in Sri Sankari Prasad Singh Deo v. Union of India and Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan. The Court also recognized that the Constitution itself provides for specified modifications or suspensions of rights in particular circumstances, including under Articles 33, 34 and 35.

predicates.constitutional_amendment_proceeding: The proceeding concerns whether Parliament may change the Constitution by amendment.
predicates.amendment_changes_part_three: The proposed amendment changes provisions protecting fundamental rights.
predicates.amendment_reduces_fundamental_rights: The amendment takes away or diminishes a fundamental right.

issues.definition: If a constitutional amendment changes fundamental-rights provisions and reduces a protected right, Parliament cannot make that reduction by amendment.

issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may limit the retrospective effect of a new constitutional ruling to preserve transactions and arrangements made in reliance on earlier decisions.
material_facts: The Court departed from earlier decisions that had permitted amendments affecting fundamental rights.
For many years, legislatures had enacted land-reform laws on the basis of those earlier decisions, and those laws had substantially changed landholding and created new titles.
The Court considered that applying its new ruling retrospectively would unsettle those arrangements and create serious disruption.
issues.conclusion: The Court applied prospective overruling, so its new rule did not invalidate the challenged amendment or other earlier amendments affecting fundamental rights.
issues.legal_principle: The Court relied on Articles 32, 141 and 142 to recognize its authority to declare law prospectively and mould relief to do complete justice. It drew on Great Northern Railway v. Sunburst Oil & Refining Co., Chicot County Drainage District v. Baxter State Bank and Linkletter v. Walker. It stated that prospective overruling may be used only in matters arising under the Constitution, only by the Supreme Court, and with the extent of retrospective operation left to the Court’s discretion according to justice in the case.

predicates.supreme_court_constitutional_case: The Supreme Court is deciding a case arising under the Constitution.
predicates.supreme_court_changes_constitutional_pre: The Supreme Court replaces an earlier constitutional rule with a new one.
predicates.prior_precedent_underpinned_widespread_r: Legislatures or others substantially relied on the earlier rule in making laws or arranging their affairs.
predicates.retroactive_change_would_disrupt_establi: Applying the new rule to the past would unsettle established transactions or create serious disruption.

issues.definition: When the Supreme Court changes a constitutional rule that supported widespread reliance and retroactive application would disrupt established arrangements, the new rule may operate prospectively.

issues.legal_issue: Land-reform statutes protected by the earlier constitutional amendment remain immune from fundamental-rights challenges after the Court applies its new rule prospectively.
material_facts: The challenged land-reform statutes had been included in the Ninth Schedule by the Seventeenth Amendment.
The Court applied its new interpretation prospectively and declared that its decision would not affect the validity of that amendment.
The parties accepted that, while the amendment remained valid, the statutes could not be challenged on the stated fundamental-rights grounds.
issues.conclusion: Because the Seventeenth Amendment remained valid, the challenged statutes could not be questioned on the ground that they infringed fundamental rights.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied prospective overruling to preserve the Seventeenth Amendment and other earlier amendments. Article 31-B provides that statutes specified in the Ninth Schedule are not void on the ground that they conflict with or abridge rights in Part III. The Court did not decide whether the challenged statutes could be sustained on any other constitutional basis.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_reform_: A party challenged land-reform statutes on constitutional grounds.
predicates.laws_were_listed_in_protected_schedule: The challenged statutes had been placed in a constitutional schedule that protects listed laws from specified rights-based challenges.
predicates.earlier_amendment_is_preserved: The constitutional amendment that provided the protection remains valid for the relevant laws.

issues.definition: If challenged land-reform laws were placed in a protected schedule by an amendment that remains valid, they cannot be attacked on fundamental-rights grounds.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge to whether Parliament acted within its constitutional power to amend is justiciable despite the political considerations behind the amendment.
material_facts: The respondents argued that constitutional amendments involved political questions outside judicial review.
The Court was asked to determine whether Parliament’s amendment power extended to changing fundamental rights.
issues.conclusion: The Court may determine whether Parliament acted within the scope of its amendment power; the political character of the reasons for an amendment does not exclude judicial review.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that jurisdiction depends on whether the Constitution expressly or by necessary implication excludes the issue from judicial determination, not on whether the issue is described as political. The Court’s task is to determine the scope of the constitutional power, rather than to decide the political merits of exercising it.

predicates.constitutional_amendment_power_contested: A proceeding disputes the extent of Parliament’s power to amend the Constitution.
predicates.party_claims_amendment_exceeds_authority: A party alleges that an amendment goes beyond the power the Constitution grants.

issues.definition: When a proceeding disputes the scope of Parliament’s amendment power and alleges that an amendment exceeds it, a court may review that issue.
